“The most critical thing for founders or earlier-stage companies to do is develop learning density or pattern recognition for where your customers are,” Arno said. “Don’t rush to build out a top-down go-to-market motion if you’re not there yet.”
That’s why, in those first 90 days after launching a commercial product that’s ready to sell, founders should not mistake early, fast revenue for a sign that the startup is ready to scale, Arno said.
Once a startup finds use cases that work, it will only be ready to build out a sales team and go for growth after it can attract new customers by repeating what has worked. If every sale requires new tactics, the startup hasn’t truly hit product-market fit.
“If I bring on 10 new customers in 10 different ways to solve 10 different problems, sure, I brought revenue in, but I don’t have a way to go scale a go-to-market,” Arno said. “If I bring three customers in with a similar motion to solve a similar problem, now I have high confidence that I can go scale.”
Lovable, the AI app-building startup, set a lot of those early benchmarks with how fast it grew, and now founders everywhere are feeling the pressure to do the same. Lovable is valued at more than $13 billion by its investors, says its ARR has passed $600 million, and has raised more than $700 million in funding to date.
“The expectations for overall execution speed are absolutely tremendous,” Tunguz said.
But Tunguz said growth like Lovable’s is still the exception, though founders should still move fast. The pressure they feel is real, he said, because far more money flows through the startup ecosystem at every stage than when he began investing in 2008. Today, a seed deal brought in by one of his partners could just as easily be a $5 million raise, a $50 million raise, or a $500 million raise.
The winners all focus on one thing: understanding their customers well enough to know what will keep them around even after any hype subsides.
“Community building is very important and being close to customers is very important,” Broca said. He said founders can send emails and throw events, and he personally likes to talk to a lot of his customers: “The general rule is always to be talking to customers.”

title_en: The trailer for Mass Effect 5 has leaked and unfortunately it looks good
title_fa: The trailer for Mass Effect 5 has leaked and unfortunately it looks good
excerpt_en: 'Mass Effect: Universe' looks like it would have focused on a new protagonist and series favorite Liara T'Soni.
excerpt_fa: 'Mass Effect: Universe' looks like it would have focused on a new protagonist and series favorite Liara T'Soni.
content_en:
The trailer for Mass Effect 5 has leaked and unfortunately it looks good
'Mass Effect: Universe' looks like it would have focused on a new protagonist and series favorite Liara T'Soni.
A trailer for BioWare's in-development Mass Effect sequel has leaked on Reddit, just as the possibility of it ever being released has all but vanished following EA's closure of the studio. The trailer was posted from a burner account by a user who claims to be an EA employee, and Bloomberg's Jason Schreier has separately confirmed the footage is the real deal in a Bluesky post.
After opening with text that notes it's made from in-game footage using pre-production assets, the trailer cuts to a man wearing an N7 trench coat (presumably the new protagonist) entering a bar, where an asari approaches him to strike up a conversation. He recounts his experience in the military before sharing that he's picked up a "new line of work," over footage of the galaxy-saving punching, shooting and kissing that should be familiar to fans of the series. After the asari threatens him, Liara T'Soni — an asari ally of the original trilogy's Commander Shepard — reveals herself and the bar breaks out into a fight. The trailer ends on the game's title: Mass Effect: Universe.
The last new Mass Effect game BioWare released was Mass Effect: Andromeda, a 2017 follow-up to Mass Effect 3 that was widely panned by fans and was reportedly the product of a troubled development process. BioWare first teased it was working on more Mass Effect in 2020, while it was still developing its next Dragon Age title. Development on the game has continued since then, through the 2021 release of Mass Effect Legendary Edition, a remastered version of the original trilogy of games, and studio layoffs before and after the release of Dragon Age: The Veilguard. Considering EA said it wouldn't continue development following BioWare's closure, this trailer is likely all we'll get to see of the game.

excerpt_fa: Oh sure, SpaceX's credit risk is pretty high because it's about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips, but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger! The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has...
content_en:
Oh sure, SpaceX’s credit risk is pretty high because it’s about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips, but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger!
Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
Yes, of course there are pay package incentives in play for Musk. But that’s not all.
Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
Yes, of course there are pay package incentives in play for Musk. But that’s not all.
The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to do with the degree to which you believe Elon Musk about wanting to go to Mars, or “spread the light of consciousness,” as he put it in this week’s SpaceX earnings call (and earlier S-1). Now, a reasonably informed person knows that we don’t have the technology — or, frankly, even the raw information to build the technology — in order to support human life in space. So that means robots. But a lag between Earth and the Moon or Mars makes for difficulty in controlling the robots. So having artificially intelligent robots who can make decisions on their own with minimal supervision from Earth is the next sci-fi logic step.
“There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”
If you believe Musk’s story, the technology we are talking about is being developed through self-driving cars (Tesla), LLMs (SpaceX), and humanoid robots (Tesla), all of which require data centers (SpaceX). Conveniently, we have just had earnings for both companies. On the other hand, if you view Mars as a useful fiction Musk uses to explain his antics in public, well, there’s a lot of money and a lot of control Musk gets from the merger.
Musk said on the recent SpaceX earnings call that “there’s a lot of merit to combining” SpaceX and Tesla. Why? “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” But artificial intelligence — ah, excuse me, super intelligence software isn’t the business SpaceX is really in right now. In its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, SpaceX reported $7.56 billion in revenue from the artificial intelligence — sorry, sorry, super intelligence division. The subcategory “SI solutions & infrastructure revenues” — which I think is Grok, Cursor, and the neocloud business wrapped together — jumped to $7 billion, or more than three times what it was last quarter. Now some of this was getting Cursor stapled on, which added $608 million in revenue. Most of the rest of that $7 billion was likely renting out compute to Anthropic and Google; Grok is probably contributing less, says Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson.
At first blush, this may look comparable to the revenue of a company like Anthropic, whose leaked S-1 shows the company had $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of this year from its frontier models. But SpaceX’s AI business looks more like CoreWeave than Anthropic. While we are told in the press release there was “increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers,” that number wasn’t broken out from bare-metal revenue. And if Musk wanted to brag about it, he would.
As for Tesla, which released Q3 results on Wednesday, its earnings sucked — a second consecutive quarter of declining profits. That’s because Musk is apparently not especially interested in normal cars anymore. Instead, Tesla is focusing on robots and, I guess, self-driving taxis. (There was also a Roadster hopping car demo recently, but that’s not going into production for a couple years, it’s very expensive, and Tesla cannot guarantee it will be delivered.) Musk did not elaborate on his comments about the merger on the Tesla call.
Macroharder
SpaceX and Tesla have some tie-ups already; SpaceX, for instance, bought $131 million of the low-selling Cybertrucks from Tesla. It has, in the past, held Tesla bonds. More crucially, the companies have also announced two AI — fuck it, we’re just sticking with AI — projects together: Terafab and Macrohard.
Terafab is the chip-making venture that Musk intends to build in Texas and run to supply himself with chips; Intel is partnered, kinda, with Musk to develop the technology. Macrohard is, uh, an AI project that lets people simulate software already made by Microsoft. At least, I think that’s what it’s supposed to be. Typing the name of the latter makes me pray for the asteroid to hit us all right now, so perhaps it’s fortunate that we haven’t heard much about it since the announcement in March.
“Musk has a history of setting timelines that his companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement
SpaceX’s S-1 from May said that Terafab and Microhard “are in the very early stages, as a result of which we and Tesla have not finalized a variety of details relating to our collaboration, including, but not limited to, financial terms, intellectual property rights, and the ultimate term of our collaboration.” As of earlier this month, Intel’s CEO said the company remained committed to the partnership, but it’s not obligated to remain part of Terafab and the S-1 says there may never be a definitive agreement. Intel’s Thomas Hannaford didn’t immediately respond to my emails asking if anything had been signed in the interim.
On this week’s call with SpaceX investors, Musk claimed the Terafab will reach volume production in the second half of 2028. He also said the company will have its first test chip from the facility in May or June 2027. “Musk has a history of setting timelines that his companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement. When an analyst on the call asked if Musk had placed orders for machines needed to make cutting-edge equipment, Musk did not answer.
Companies often are doing more privately than they announce publicly, so I do not view the S-1 filing as fully definitive. But Macrohard isn’t mentioned in the last 10Q. Neither is Terafab.

title_en: 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
title_fa: 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
excerpt_en: The new feature allows agents to log into a customer's personal accounts while still protecting the private credentials that secure those accounts.
excerpt_fa: The new feature allows agents to log into a customer's personal accounts while still protecting the private credentials that secure those accounts.
content_en:
Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up.
Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials.
The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents, accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand.
1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service.
“Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post. “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.”
Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts.
This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not.
Bankers interviewed by the outlet described the situation as “horrifying,” and a Chase spokesperson interviewed by Axios additionally told the outlet that customers “should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone.”

title_en: 2027 BMW iX5 first drive: You'll love the range, but maybe not the look
title_fa: 2027 BMW iX5 first drive: You'll love the range, but maybe not the look
excerpt_en: BMW's latest EV will do over 450 miles on a charge and even close its own doors.
excerpt_fa: BMW's latest EV will do over 450 miles on a charge and even close its own doors.
content_en:
2027 BMW iX5 first drive: You'll love the range, but maybe not the look
BMW's latest EV will do over 450 miles on a charge and even close its own doors.
Too many manufacturers are getting too clever in trying to reinvent the humble door handle lately, sometimes with fatal consequences. BMW is certainly joining that crowd with the upcoming electric SUV, the iX5. It's the effective replacement for the iX, the next step up the model line from the recently released iX3, and a battery-powered alternative to the two-row X5.
The iX5 has little winglets at the top of the front and rear doors containing strain meters that can detect a subtle pull without actually flexing. It's a vastly complex system that enables something surprisingly nice: power doors that actually work.
Reinventing the door handle
Pull the little winglet and the door swings itself open as far as it can, relying on embedded sensors to avoid slamming into you or the car you parked next to. Get inside, step on the brake pedal and the door quickly closes itself. This isn't novel technology by any means. A fair few cars (mostly expensive ones) have offered this in the past, but I tend to find them extremely annoying.
Most are so slow that I never want to wait for them, so sluggish that they're hard to close manually or so unreliable that I couldn't trust them to not create a power-assisted ding into the next car over. In the iX5, they actually work, adding a little more luxury to the electric version of BMW's second-best-selling machine in the US.
It's far from the only luxurious touch. The SUV I drove was the 570-horsepower, 593-pound-foot iX5 60 xDrive model, outfitted with plush, massaging seats. The matte silver paint on the outside gave it a premium look, even if the styling is polarizing, to say the least.
A shared safety experience
The driver assistance system also has some decidedly premium touches. BMW evocatively calls it "Symbiotic Drive," and though that sounds vaguely alien and ominous, it just means that the system works with you. On the highway it'll steer itself, and you can take your hands off the wheel. But if you want to change lanes, you can either tap the turn stalk, or just grab the wheel and execute the change, then let it go again.
You can speed up and even slow down manually without the system disengaging, something that definitely takes some getting used to. This isn't like an old-school cruise control system that turns off the second you touch the brake pedal or launches itself up to full speed as soon as it's engaged. You can apply the brake to bring yourself to a complete stop for a light, then lift off again and the car will smoothly resume.
It works excellently, as does the infotainment system, which runs on a curiously inclined, 17.9-inch touchscreen in the center of the dashboard. Everything is quick and responsive, and though the integrated AI assistant was a little over-eager to chime in whenever anyone in the car said "BMW," it was at least able to find restaurants and answers to all of the inane queries we expect from our agentic future overlords.
Panoramic Vision
Above that touchscreen, situated far back on the dashboard, is BMW's Panoramic Vision display. It runs from pillar to pillar, with six segments that you can customize to show everything from the current weather to arbitrary pictures of vintage BMWs. It looks a bit much at first, but it's actually quite nice to have, and is a lot easier to see than your average gauge cluster hidden behind the steering wheel.
It's certainly more useful than the final display in the iX5, the optional 14.6-inch passenger display. This is situated to the right and slightly behind the central display, to obscure it from the driver's view. That's because BMW opted not to use the same kind of perspective-limiting display technology that many other premium SUVs have used.
Instead, the system relies on the driver-monitoring camera to detect when the driver's gaze wanders to the passenger display. When it does, the screen goes blank and whatever video the passenger is watching pauses. The screen turns back on again when the driver looks away, but the passenger has to manually resume the video. As far as user experiences go, it's not ideal.
Range-topper
The iX5's most luxurious feature might be the range. The iX5 carries a prodigious 144-kilowatt-hour battery slung down below the passenger compartment. It charges at a remarkable 460kW via NACS port, enough to get from 10 to 80 percent in 22 minutes if you can find a charger with enough juice.
BMW hasn't completed its EPA testing, but says to expect more than 450 miles on a charge. To prove that's attainable, one of BMW's engineers drove over 500 miles from San Francisco to LA without stopping and still had 50 miles remaining.
My road trip was a fair bit shorter, but I did spend about six hours behind the wheel of a pair of BMW's new SUVs. The first half I was in the X5 40 xDrive, the internal combustion version. The second half was in the electric, and it was my clear preference.
Though the gasoline-burning X5 had good power at higher speeds and made a nice sound when I floored it, the throttle response on the iX5 was infinitely sharper. It is certainly heavier, but the lower center of gravity made it feel that much more engaging in the corners, and it can do the same stopping trick as the iX3, relying on the electric motors to come to a standstill so smoothly that if you close your eyes you literally can't tell when the wheels stop rolling.
Wrap-up
But there's honestly not much between the gas-powered X5 and battery-powered iX5. That's a big change of positioning compared to the even more polarizing iX and the prior-generation X5. Though similar in many regards, those two looked and drove nothing alike.
For this generation, BMW is bringing the family together, making the internal combustion and battery-electric versions look nigh identical. They're even pricing them similarly, with the plug-in X5 50e starting at...

It looks a bit much at first, but it's actually quite nice to have, and is a lot easier to see than your average gauge cluster hidden behind the steering wheel.
It's certainly more useful than the final display in the iX5, the optional 14.6-inch passenger display. This is situated to the right and slightly behind the central display, to obscure it from the driver's view. That's because BMW opted not to use the same kind of perspective-limiting display technology that many other premium SUVs have used.
Instead, the system relies on the driver-monitoring camera to detect when the driver's gaze wanders to the passenger display. When it does, the screen goes blank and whatever video the passenger is watching pauses. The screen turns back on again when the driver looks away, but the passenger has to manually resume the video. As far as user experiences go, it's not ideal.
Range-topper
The iX5's most luxurious feature might be the range. The iX5 carries a prodigious 144-kilowatt-hour battery slung down below the passenger compartment. It charges at a remarkable 460kW via NACS port, enough to get from 10 to 80 percent in 22 minutes if you can find a charger with enough juice.
BMW hasn't completed its EPA testing, but says to expect more than 450 miles on a charge. To prove that's attainable, one of BMW's engineers drove over 500 miles from San Francisco to LA without stopping and still had 50 miles remaining.
My road trip was a fair bit shorter, but I did spend about six hours behind the wheel of a pair of BMW's new SUVs. The first half I was in the X5 40 xDrive, the internal combustion version. The second half was in the electric, and it was my clear preference.
Though the gasoline-burning X5 had good power at higher speeds and made a nice sound when I floored it, the throttle response on the iX5 was infinitely sharper. It is certainly heavier, but the lower center of gravity made it feel that much more engaging in the corners, and it can do the same stopping trick as the iX3, relying on the electric motors to come to a standstill so smoothly that if you close your eyes you literally can't tell when the wheels stop rolling.
Wrap-up
But there's honestly not much between the gas-powered X5 and battery-powered iX5. That's a big change of positioning compared to the even more polarizing iX and the prior-generation X5. Though similar in many regards, those two looked and drove nothing alike.
For this generation, BMW is bringing the family together, making the internal combustion and battery-electric versions look nigh identical. They're even pricing them similarly, with the plug-in X5 50e starting at...

title_en: Canva releases its first image generation model
title_fa: Canva releases its first image generation model
excerpt_en: Canva is making its new image model available to all users, promising better, more customizable performance at lower costs.
excerpt_fa: Canva is making its new image model available to all users, promising better, more customizable performance at lower costs.
content_en:
Design platform Canva released its first image generation model, called Canva Craft, developed by its research team to compete with same-category models from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta.
The company said its model works in two stages. In the first stage, it interprets users’ prompts and creates a plan with details like spatial relationships of elements, relative scale, visual hierarchy, and information for text generation. In the second stage, its model generates an image of up to 2K resolution in a possible 30 different aspect ratios for various platforms.
Canva said that this approach allows it to create images with accurate details of objects and legible text. Plus, users would be able to make precise edits without changing other parts of the image.
The company noted that rather than using photographs, it used designs to train this model using human-designed templates from Canva’s library, including posters, social posts, presentations, infographics, menus, and typography-rich layouts.
That means images generated with Canva Craft could be converted into layered designs using Canva Magic, the company’s image-to-design transformer. Last year, the platform released its own model that understands designs and layers.
Canva Craft is available on the company’s platform to all users, who can access the model from the Dream Lab tab. The model will also be available through the Canva API. Plus, the company plans to support image generation in third-party chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini through Canva’s MCP.
Canva has used a bunch of image models for generation in its platform, so it’s likely that the new models will help save API costs for the company. It said that besides costs, the new model also allows the platform to have better quality and speed control.
In 2024, Canva acquired media generation platform Leonardo.ai. It said that the researchers from Leonardo contributed to the new image model.
Canva said that it is developing two cost-efficient versions of the model, called Craftfast and Craft-ultrafast, which will be released soon.
The company was on track for $4 billion in revenue last year. However, it cut its growth forecast for 2026, causing its valuation to reportedly plummet from $42 billion to $35 billion, according to external analysts.

title_en: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up
title_fa: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up
excerpt_en: OpenAI is launching its decision model to the world. Can it compete with the original Jev?
excerpt_fa: OpenAI is launching its decision model to the world. Can it compete with the original Jev?
content_en:
OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company.
TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost.
Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost.
“The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.”
Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically.
In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness.
Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements.
Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter.
The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan, a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.”
Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well.
Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?”
As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them.

title_en: Daft Punk is getting an official Lego set
title_fa: Daft Punk is getting an official Lego set
excerpt_en: A fan-built model of the Alive tour pyramid got the green light to become a real product.
excerpt_fa: A fan-built model of the Alive tour pyramid got the green light to become a real product.
content_en:
Daft Punk is getting an official Lego set
A fan-built model of the Alive tour pyramid got the green light to become a real product.
Daft Punk is getting the Lego treatment — officially, this time. An upcoming Lego set will pay tribute to the duo's 2007 Alive tour pyramid. The official product is an evolution of a fan-built model that won Lego's Music to Our Ears contest in 2020.
Daft Punk and Lego first teased the news on the duo's "WDPK 83.7" YouTube stream, showing a red holographic speaker/Lego brick. A short video accompanying the full announcement shows the duo's minifigures following the same laser brick into a dark landscape, where their console conveniently materializes. Head-bobbing commences, with "Voyager" and "Human After All" making up the soundtrack.
The original set was a COVID-era lockdown project by a father and son from Luxembourg. Their glowing pyramid stage includes about 2,000 pieces. A motorized, rotating box of transparent bricks sits inside, recreating the look and feel of the tour's stage spectacle. Lego's designers are working with fan creator Patrick Harboun, who goes by RobotRock, on the final version.
This likely won't be the last time the robot DJs show up in Lego. The company's marketing chief, Julia Goldin, described the announcement as "just the beginning of a bigger journey — a creative collab made for fans ready to lose themselves to play." This wasn't even the French duo's first appearance as Lego men: they had a cameo performing "Get Lucky" in the 2024 Lego-animated Pharrell Williams film, Piece By Piece.
Lego hasn't yet announced any specific details about the set, including its price or release date. However, it teased that more news will come in 2027.

title_en: The Browser Company is officially killing Arc on December 22
title_fa: The Browser Company is officially killing Arc on December 22
excerpt_en: The organization is prioritizing an AI browser called Dia.
excerpt_fa: The organization is prioritizing an AI browser called Dia.
content_en:
The Browser Company is officially killing Arc on December 22
The organization is prioritizing an AI browser called Dia.
The Browser Company will sunset its Arc browser on December 22. We kind of knew this was coming, as the company has been focusing its resources on an AI browser called Dia. To that end, the organization is trying to get users to switch over from Arc to Dia. It says that all bookmarks, extensions, passwords and history will transfer over automatically. The Browser Company is also trying to lure in customers who are wary of AI by noting that all of those additional features are optional.
As for Arc, it goes dark on December 22. On that date, users will no longer be able to access their accounts. I guess it never quite caught on, even though it offered people the ability to personalize any website while browsing.
Meet @diabrowser. Now available for Arc members. pic.twitter.com/dqekJNWhgR
— The Browser Company (@browsercompany) June 11, 2025
Dia was first announced last year and is, more or less, a standard AI-based web browser. There's a chatbot that the company says can understand context across multiple open tabs. The app can also do stuff like summarize emails and YouTube videos. It pulls together a "morning brief" each day that integrates data from calendars, inboxes and web links. You know the drill. It's generative AI.

title_en: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’
title_fa: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’
excerpt_en: Microsoft’s new AI diagnostic system beat generalist doctors on hard cases, according to a study in Science. But most of the improvement seems to come from the AI models underneath, not from Microsoft’s system itself.
excerpt_fa: Microsoft’s new AI diagnostic system beat generalist doctors on hard cases, according to a study in Science. But most of the improvement seems to come from the AI models underneath, not from Microsoft’s system itself.
content_en:
Microsoft’s AI diagnostic system correctly diagnosed complex medical cases in a simulation more than twice as often as generalist physicians, according to a study published Thursday in Science. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI’s CEO, called the result a step toward “medical superintelligence.”
The system, dubbed MAI-DxO (DxO for short), coordinates several AI agents that act like a panel of doctors. They question a patient, order tests, and debate a diagnosis.
In a simulation using complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, it was correct 83% of the time. Primary care doctors and general internists, working individually with reference materials, were correct 36% of the time. One note: Cases this complex are usually handled by specialists or physician teams, who weren’t part of the comparison.
“There is something very substantial and exciting here,” Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, told TechCrunch. “The biggest challenge in healthcare delivery at the moment is the growing mismatch between demand and supply of medical expertise.”
In publishing these results, Microsoft joins Google and OpenAI in claiming that its AI can match or outperform doctors.
The study’s own data suggests that much of the improvement comes from more powerful underlying AI models, with Microsoft’s orchestration system adding gains on top.
Microsoft tested MAI-DxO with models from several companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, but its best results came with OpenAI’s GPT-5 and GPT-5.5.
Microsoft measured DxO on cost as well as accuracy, meaning the estimated cost of running the AI on each case. On its own with a short, basic prompt, GPT-5 scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case. DxO cut that cost by about $3,000 but raised accuracy by only about four points. On emergency department cases, there was little improvement in either accuracy or cost improvement between GPT-5 on its own and with the assist from DxO.
With GPT-5.5, a newer model released in April 2026, the results split. On complex cases, DxO increased GPT-5.5’s accuracy score from 72% to nearly 87% at a slightly cheaper cost. However, the gains once again didn’t show up on emergency department cases. Both (with and without DxO) scored about 85% at a similar cost.
DxO helps most on complex cases and with less capable AI models. Gemini 2.5 Flash, for example, scored 46.4% on its own but nearly 69% with DxO. Even so, the gap between the weaker and stronger models was larger than the boost DxO provided.
Microsoft’s researchers said that accuracy gains naturally shrink as models approach the theoretical maximum. “The DxO orchestration helps with the broader challenge of optimization both accuracy and cost,” a spokesperson added.
Suleyman, who leads Microsoft’s effort to build its own frontier AI, told TechCrunch that the company is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a foundation model for healthcare, with release planned for next year. He believes this model will enable the company to “make really enormous leaps here,” and says DxO is part of the foundational infrastructure Microsoft is building to see real breakthroughs in healthcare.
“I really believe that in 2027, we will be on the verge of a coding style breakthrough for medical records,” Suleyman said. “I think we’re going to be able to stream highly accurate predictions about how a medical record might unfold, and obviously that kind of foresight for a clinician is gold dust.”
Suleyman has spent his career trying to use AI to solve medical issues. He was previously a co-founder of DeepMind, which was acquired by Google in 2014. The following year, Google DeepMind acquired King’s startup Hark, a clinical task management app, and the two of them launched DeepMind Health together. Suleyman joined Microsoft to lead its AI unit in 2024, and King followed a few months later.
“We’re just true believers,” Suleyman said.
He said while the use of generative AI in healthcare is still early, he expects healthcare models to get “an order of magnitude better in capability within the next 24 to 36 months.”
“As we’ve seen multiple times in the last five or six years, the progress happens very quickly once you have a flywheel,” Suleyman said. “A flywheel means we have a model in production which we are iterating with real-world usage in order to identify gaps in the model and then patch them and improve them. That’s what’s happened in coding. It’s what happened in chat before that. And I think next year it’s going to start to happen for medical records and for clinical decision support.”
Through a new partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Microsoft will evaluate the clinical reasoning capabilities of DxO across different hospital settings.
“This technology is ready for real-world evaluations, and you can imagine the complexity and diversity of issues that come from a Boston emergency department on a Friday evening,” King said.
He explained how the study will work: Patients will get standard treatment, including triage, time with a specialist, treatments, investigations, and decision on whether it’s safe to discharge. In parallel, those who consent will also engage with DxO. Microsoft and its partners will compare DxO’s recommendations against the human doctors’.
Google published a clinical study alongside Beth Israel in The Lancet this month to evaluate Google’s AMIE conversational diagnostic AI in real-world urgent care visits, while human physicians monitored the interactions in real time.
“We think this will be the biggest study of its kind,” King said. “It will be across not just emergency settings but urgent care environments, and will give us very compelling evidence by the end of the study period around the ability for these systems to be deployed at greater scale in the future.”

In parallel, those who consent will also engage with DxO. Microsoft and its partners will compare DxO’s recommendations against the human doctors’.
Google published a clinical study alongside Beth Israel in The Lancet this month to evaluate Google’s AMIE conversational diagnostic AI in real-world urgent care visits, while human physicians monitored the interactions in real time.
“We think this will be the biggest study of its kind,” King said. “It will be across not just emergency settings but urgent care environments, and will give us very compelling evidence by the end of the study period around the ability for these systems to be deployed at greater scale in the future.”

title_en: Former OpenAI science lead launches Warp Science to automate wet labs with robots
title_fa: Former OpenAI science lead launches Warp Science to automate wet labs with robots
excerpt_en: Wearing cameras and sensor gloves, the startup’s human chemists will train robots to perform various lab tasks.
excerpt_fa: Wearing cameras and sensor gloves, the startup’s human chemists will train robots to perform various lab tasks.
content_en:
Former OpenAI science lead Kevin Weil has launched Warp Sciences, a new AI startup focused on automating lab work for drug discovery. The company, which trains robots to make and test promising compounds identified by researchers, has raised $215 million at an $865 million valuation, according to Weil, who announced the startup and funding on X.
The round was led by Lightspeed, with participation from IVP, Mayfield, Lux Capital, Premji Invest, and Menlo Ventures.
For years, biotech companies have outsourced the most labor-intensive work of synthesizing thousands of variations of molecules to contractors in China, such as WuXi AppTec. With Warp Sciences, Weil hopes to reshore that work and insulate the entire drug development process from geopolitical supply-chain risks.
Wearing cameras and sensor gloves, the startup’s human chemists will train robots to perform various lab tasks. By automating wet-lab work, Warp Sciences aims to accelerate drug discovery using robots that can operate around the clock.

title_en: Bluesky adds iPad support in latest feature update
title_fa: Bluesky adds iPad support in latest feature update
excerpt_en: Profile links to third-party platforms have also arrived on the social network.
excerpt_fa: Profile links to third-party platforms have also arrived on the social network.
content_en:
Bluesky adds iPad support in latest feature update
Profile links to third-party platforms have also arrived on the social network.
Bluesky rolled out several features in its latest update, notably beta testing support for iPads. The social network should start looking and performing better on the Apple tablets as a result of the changes. The Beta Features section of the Settings menu can be used to share feedback about any bugs or wonkiness found in the Bluesky iPad app.
Another update is aimed at self-promotion. Bluesky users can now put links to external platforms at the top of their profiles. The company framed the addition as a way for creators to get better support from their Bluesky audiences by connecting their profiles to crowdfunding platforms such as Patreon or Ko-fi or to more of their content in a website or newsletter. This might also cut down on some of the "link in bio" language that's so common in many social media posts. The Edit Profile menu now has a Links section where those external sites can be added.

title_en: Amazon rebrands Kindle Unlimited to Kindle+
title_fa: Amazon rebrands Kindle Unlimited to Kindle+
excerpt_en: The service still offers a library of books, magazines and comics, and now includes a larger selection of audiobooks.
excerpt_fa: The service still offers a library of books, magazines and comics, and now includes a larger selection of audiobooks.
content_en:
Amazon rebrands Kindle Unlimited to Kindle+
The service still offers a library of books, magazines and comics, and now includes a larger selection of audiobooks.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
You exist long enough as a subscription service, and eventually you'll get a "+." Kindle Unlimited, Amazon's subscription service for borrowing books, comics and magazines, is the latest service to fall. In an email to subscribers, Amazon said it's renaming the subscription to Kindle+ and expanding its library of audiobooks.
The service still offers access to the same reading material, and now "thousands more audiobooks," according to Amazon. Amazon also says reading history, bookmarks, notes and saved titles all carry over to Kindle+, and it'll still cost $12 per month and limit borrowing to 20 titles at a time.
Really, the only thing that's meaningfully changing is the audiobook library. One of the ways Amazon is expanding its existing collection is by allowing authors who self-publish through the company's Kindle Direct Publishing platform to include their audiobooks in the service. Self-published authors have the option to upload traditionally produced audiobooks, and Amazon is also testing a service that can generate audiobooks read by a "virtual voice."
Kindle+ is live now and should work just as well through Amazon's Kindle app as it does on the company's redesigned lineup of Kindle hardware.

title_en: Unauthorized AI agents are reportedly already accessing US bank accounts
title_fa: Unauthorized AI agents are reportedly already accessing US bank accounts
excerpt_en: Sources at several banks have indicated that they have been taking actions independent of user instructions.
excerpt_fa: Sources at several banks have indicated that they have been taking actions independent of user instructions.
content_en:
Unauthorized AI agents are reportedly already accessing US bank accounts
Sources at several banks have indicated that they have been taking actions independent of user instructions.
Unauthorized third-party AI agents are accessing US bank accounts, according to a report by Axios. Some of these agents are even taking actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, though this is based on unnamed sources within several banking institutions.
Many AI agents, including the cute and cuddly Muse, can access a user's bank account to perform actions on their behalf. This is already a security nightmare, as most banks mandate that humans log in to their own accounts. The problem is compounded when these agents start to buy things or shift money around. The potential for scams and fraud is off the charts.
Banks have tracked agent activity and suggested that they have done things like contact call centers, all without being given specific permission. This has caused institutions like Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo to rapidly make changes to contain any risk. Some have blocked third-party agents from accessing their platforms and others have issued restrictions in certain instances. Many are trying to make it so agents only have read access and cannot actually make any changes.
A Chase spokesperson told Axios that customers should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone, and that includes AI agents. CEO Jamie Dimon also warned in a recent earnings call that there could be thousands of rogue agents operating across financial platforms.
There haven't been too many stories of AI-induced financial calamity just yet, but it's worth exercising some prudence before letting these agents run amok in your bank account. That's because it's highly unlikely you'd get your money back if an agent did do something wrong. The banks wouldn't be liable for restitution, as it would be considered a voluntary action on the part of the user. This is according to laws like the US Electronic Fund Transfer Act. It's not fraud if you're the one handing over the keys to AI. In other words, be careful out there.

title_en: Elon Musk made a $1B investment in Skydance, report says
title_fa: Elon Musk made a $1B investment in Skydance, report says
excerpt_en: The investment will provide a much-needed financial boost as the company seeks to cut costs and lift its stock price.
excerpt_fa: The investment will provide a much-needed financial boost as the company seeks to cut costs and lift its stock price.
content_en:
Elon Musk has invested approximately $1 billion in the newly formed media company Skydance, according to a new report from Semafor. News of the investment comes a few weeks after Paramount completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery to create the combined company.
Co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz are tasked with bringing together two major streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max, along with a portfolio of networks, including CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, and Food Network, under a single corporate umbrella.
Semafor reports that Musk’s investment was made around the same time as equity contributions from other Skydance investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs. The investment will provide a much needed financial boost as the company seeks to cut costs and lift its stock price, the report notes.
Skydance has already committed to reducing costs by $6 billion over the next three years.
Musk has publicly praised the Ellisons in the past and has close ties with Larry Ellison, whom he appointed to Tesla’s board of directors in 2018. The Oracle founder invested $1 billion to help Musk purchase Twitter in 2022 and also invested in Tesla in 2018.
Skydance did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

title_en: Chinese hackers spied on thousands of companies after breaching IT giant ConnectWise
title_fa: Chinese hackers spied on thousands of companies after breaching IT giant ConnectWise
excerpt_en: Microsoft points the blame for ConnectWise's breach at a China-aligned hacker, which relied on AI agents to rapidly hack into thousands of its customers.
excerpt_fa: Microsoft points the blame for ConnectWise's breach at a China-aligned hacker, which relied on AI agents to rapidly hack into thousands of its customers.
content_en:
The bad week for cybersecurity just got worse for thousands more companies, who were spied on by Chinese hackers following the breach of IT management and remote access giant ConnectWise.
Security researchers at Microsoft say the China state-aligned hackers broke into ConnectWise’s cloud backup service and stole application credentials that are used to establish data links between ConnectWise and its corporate customers, who rely on the cloud service to back up their company’s data.
By stealing the credentials, the hackers could log in to the customer’s Microsoft-hosted environment as if they were an authorized user and access their emails and other files.
According to Microsoft, the hackers used AI agents to rapidly hack into around 2,250 organizations at a rate of almost 3,000 attempted sign-ins per minute. Microsoft said this speed gives defenders “little time to detect and respond.”
The speed of the mass-hacks was attributed to the use of AI agents, specifically ARTEX, an open source AI framework that works with AI models to stress-test cyber defenses. The same AI software was used in a recent compromise of South Korea’s financial systems, many of which had weak security and lacked multi-factor authentication.
ConnectWise said it’s paused access to its cloud backup system and is investigating the breach. As of Thursday, the company said it was working on restoring the service.

title_en: Sundar Pichai (allegedly) draws the line at oceans
title_fa: Sundar Pichai (allegedly) draws the line at oceans
excerpt_en: President Trump claimed that the Google CEO refused to rename the Atlantic Ocean in Maps.
excerpt_fa: President Trump claimed that the Google CEO refused to rename the Atlantic Ocean in Maps.
content_en:
Sundar Pichai (allegedly) draws the line at oceans
President Trump claimed that the Google CEO refused to rename the Atlantic Ocean in Maps.
Capitulating to a bully might seem like a good idea in the short term. But do it once, and you've proven that you'll acquiesce to an escalating series of demands. Take Google, for example. The company, which appeased Trump by renaming the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario in Google Maps, has (allegedly) had to field a call about renaming the Atlantic Ocean.
That's the scenario President Trump recounted at a rally on Wednesday in South Carolina. He said he called Google CEO Sundar Pichai to ask whether Google Maps could "handle" a new name for the Atlantic. The president said he'd weighed whether to use "Trump" or "America" on either the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean. Pichai's response was, reportedly, "Please don't ask us to do that."
According to Trump, Google's compliance finally hit a limit. "No, no, no, this time I'm not doing it," Trump quoted the CEO as saying. "Oceans are different, sir." The stated rationale was that oceans "cover a lot of countries." Of course, the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario also touch more than one country: three for the former and two for the latter.
Trump said he'd "probably pass" on the Atlantic. However, he also floated renaming the Pacific Ocean "the American Ocean" instead.
Google didn't stumble into this. In early 2025, it relabeled the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America" for US users following Trump's executive order. This August, it did the same to Lake Ontario in the US, which now reads as "Lake America." In both cases, Apple followed suit. It's increasingly clear just how low Big Tech will stoop when tariff exemptions, regulatory favors and government contracts are on the line.
Meanwhile, inflation is rising, gas is at $4.27 a gallon and diesel is at $6.31, according to AAA. The Iran war has dragged on for 236 days despite Trump suggesting in March that it could be over in four to five weeks. With the midterms less than two weeks away, at least we have a president who's laser-focused on the real issues.
We reached out to Google for comment and will update this story if we hear back.

title_en: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 Startup Battlefield 200: Celebrating outstanding achievements
title_fa: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 Startup Battlefield 200: Celebrating outstanding achievements
excerpt_en: Among the Startup Battlefield 200 were many industry-defining companies exhibiting and pitching on the Showcase Stage. Here are the standouts.
excerpt_fa: Among the Startup Battlefield 200 were many industry-defining companies exhibiting and pitching on the Showcase Stage. Here are the standouts.
content_en:
This year, TechCrunch Disrupt showcased the incredible talent and groundbreaking ideas of our 2026 Startup Battlefield 200 cohort.
Out of thousands of applications, we selected 200 of the most promising startups, each bringing unique innovations to their respective industries. The competition culminated in an electrifying event where these startups had the opportunity to pitch and demonstrate their solutions live over three days.
From the top 20 finalists, TechCrunch editorial selected the top five companies that then battled it out for the $100,000 equity-free prize and the coveted Disrupt Cup. The well-deserved win went to Intero Biosystems, with a strong runner-up, Apate.
Among the Startup Battlefield 200 were many industry-defining companies exhibiting and pitching on the Showcase Stage. Here are the standouts:
Best Showcase Stage pitch by industry group
Built World
Lola Vision Systems provides a full-stack AI platform delivering sensor fusion, secure communications, and real-time inference on today’s hardware, with purpose-built silicon on the horizon.
Sustainability
Krokos Bio is growing nature’s most valuable ingredients, in a way that is cheaper and more reliable, starting with saffron.
Enterprise Group 1
Rein Security is the security layer for custom-built enterprise agents — the production AI agents running businesses worldwide.
Enterprise Group 2
Lumai is the optical compute company addressing scalable AI in the inference era.
Health
Uhura Bionics has developed a bionic larynx for singing, laughing, and translating emotions.
Consumer
Maka is delivering developmentally curated shows parents trust and kids love — powered by AI.
Best Booth
Legali AI is providing a trauma-informed AI legal companion and ecosystem for the middle class and AI-native firms, with a focus on women who’ve faced abuse. Their all-pink, female-focused booth was a standout on the Expo Floor. Visitors would write empowering messages to women on sticky notes and place them on Legali AI’s banner while learning more about the wonderful work they’re doing. Founder Ira Puteri also made a point of coordinating different pink outfits each day. Love the commitment!
Spirit of Disrupt award
The Spirit of Disrupt award unanimously goes to Shogher Atanesyan, founder and CEO of Ardook Data. Her journey to the Startup Battlefield 200 is inspiring, with her first exposure to Disrupt as a volunteer back in 2023. She had reached out to the Battlefield team last year, with a simple request to make “Social Impact” a stand-alone category in the Event App. We were happy to oblige, and just a few short months later she applied for the competition. She made it in on her own merits, as the review team loved the concept of capturing real-world household training data from a willing and paid caregiver network. The data is then sold to physical AI and robotics companies in need of it.
Atanesyan may be the most selfless founder we’ve seen in five years of managing the Startup Battlefield 200. Specifically, what she did for visitors to San Francisco. She organized dozens of student volunteers to help these startups manage their booths, coordinated numerous items shipped to her house to circumvent steep shipping costs, and hosted a party for these founders at her house. Additionally, she consistently helped founders who had questions in our community Discord and weekly calls.
The Startup Battlefield is more than a pitch competition; it’s an opportunity to build relationships with investors, potential customers, and fellow founders to support each other on their entrepreneurial journeys.
As we celebrate the achievements of this year’s winners, we are excited to see how they will shape their industries and drive innovation in the months and years to come. Congratulations to all the participants of the Startup Battlefield 200, and a special thank-you to our judges and sponsors for their support in making TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 a resounding success.

title_en: Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work
title_fa: Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work
excerpt_en: The ride-share giant previously deployed a much smaller pilot for ChatGPT Work but is now taking the enterprise agent company-wide.
excerpt_fa: The ride-share giant previously deployed a much smaller pilot for ChatGPT Work but is now taking the enterprise agent company-wide.
content_en:
Uber and OpenAI announced an expansion of their partnership on Thursday, with the ride-share giant telling TechCrunch that its entire global workforce — some 30,000 people — will now be using ChatGPT Work.
ChatGPT Work was introduced in July as an enterprise-focused AI agent that corporate teams could deploy for various workflows.
Uber originally piloted ChatGPT Work with 1,000 employees earlier this year but has now scaled up its usage to the entire company.
That earlier pilot was deployed to workers from across Uber’s various departments, including finance, operations, and product. Indeed, a majority of the early adopters — some 80% — were non-engineers, Sumanth Sukumar, Uber’s VP of engineering, told TechCrunch.
“They used it for a wide range of tasks: analyzing complex data from our operations to identify trends and develop recommendations; localizing training materials for different markets and languages; and building personalized interactive dashboards to manage their daily work,” he said.
Yet while the ride-share giant is now going all in on ChatGPT, it has not settled on exactly how employees will use it. “Our approach is to make powerful AI tools available across Uber while giving teams room to experiment,” Sukumar said. “For example, earlier this year we paired 30 AI engineers with teams across Uber and gave them two weeks to automate key parts of their job. Those ‘AI pods’ showed us how much opportunity there is when you combine technical expertise with a deep understanding of a particular job.”
Uber didn’t disclose how much it’s spending on the new rollout of the chatbot. Instead, Sukumar said the company will track how employees use the tool. “We’ll look at how employees are using the technology, the kinds of workflows they develop and how it helps them work more effectively. We’ll evaluate those outcomes and use what we learn to guide how we deploy AI across the business,” he said. Uber says OpenAI worked closely with the company on integrating the chatbot.
OpenAI has moved quickly to scale up its enterprise business as it competes with its chief competitor, Anthropic. Once known largely as a consumer brand, the ChatGPT creator has swiftly gained a loyal following with business customers, while other AI companies have struggled to keep up.

title_en: PC shipments are in the toilet, plunging over 20 percent from last year
title_fa: PC shipments are in the toilet, plunging over 20 percent from last year
excerpt_en: This could reach 27 percent throughout the end of 2026 as prices continue to rise.
excerpt_fa: This could reach 27 percent throughout the end of 2026 as prices continue to rise.
content_en:
PC shipments are in the toilet, plunging over 20 percent from last year
This could reach 27 percent throughout the end of 2026.
Global PC shipments are down 21 percent year-over-year for Q3, according to data accumulated by the market research firm Counterpoint. The industry shipped over 70 million units during this time period last year, but that number has shriveled to 57 million.
As a matter of fact, there's been a quarter-over-quarter reduction of 13.8 percent, suggesting that this downturn is moving quite rapidly. Counterpoint's data has also indicated that this trend will continue, with forecasts for Q4 indicating around a 27 percent reduction year-over-year.
It's not hard to understand why this is happening. PC components keep shooting up in price, thanks to both the ongoing AI-induced RAMageddon and global tariffs, and many people just can't keep up.
"The global PC market is facing mounting pressure as rising memory and component costs push system prices higher and force consumers to delay replacement purchases," said Counterpoint senior analyst Minsoo Kang. "With affordability becoming an increasingly critical purchasing factor, even market leaders are struggling to maintain shipment momentum."
There's only one tiny sliver of potential sunshine here. These numbers are absolutely dire, yes, but 2025 was actually a great year for PC shipments. The same goes for early 2026, as consumers raced to pick up new computers before prices shot up. Everyone knew this was coming and acted accordingly. Hopefully consumers will come back when prices for memory and other components fall back down to Earth.
However, that probably won't be anytime soon. Counterpoint's research has suggested 2027 will be more of the same.
Some companies are surviving this better than others. Lenovo is still the market leader, though it has experienced a higher-than-average 23 percent year-over-year decline. HP experienced a massive 31 percent decline during that same time period, with Dell at 25 percent.
Apple, however, experienced a smaller decline of 11 percent, which actually increased the company's overall market share. This is likely thanks to the budget-friendly MacBook Neo. ASUS has also managed to weather the storm, more or less. The company recorded the smallest decline when compared to other top vendors, at just seven percent year-over-year.
A 20.1% decline in worldwide PC shipments tells part of the story. The inventory pull-in underneath it tells the rest.
Q3 normally beats Q2. In 2026, it came in 9.1% below.
Full Q3 results: https://t.co/Fa1nhvsU0a#PCMarket #PCShipments #IDCResearch pic.twitter.com/J9OIYx4Shy
— IDC (@IDC) October 8, 2026
Counterpoint is just one firm that's tracking this kind of thing. The International Data Corporation recently reported similar numbers for Q3.

title_en: Tesla is prepping a Cybercab onslaught
title_fa: Tesla is prepping a Cybercab onslaught
excerpt_en: The company is looking to roll out the gold two-seater robotaxis to other U.S. cities this year, even as it goes mum on the number of paid rides.
excerpt_fa: The company is looking to roll out the gold two-seater robotaxis to other U.S. cities this year, even as it goes mum on the number of paid rides.
content_en:
Tesla says it is preparing to launch its shiny gold Cybercab in new markets outside its home of Austin, Texas, in a bid to “literally take over every part of terrestrial transportation.”
“We’re starting with getting people from one place to the other, but we want to basically own transportation of any kind on Earth,” Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday.
Tesla has previously shown a concept version of a multi-passenger vehicle it calls the “Robovan,” but it’s unclear if Taneja’s bombastic comments mean the company is working on other types of transportation.
What was clearer on the call is that Tesla’s Cybercab expansion will begin in Dallas next month and spread to other cities by the end of this year. Tesla already operates robotaxi versions of its Model Y SUV in small fleets in Dallas, Houston, and the Florida cities of Miami, Orlando, and Tampa. The company also said on its earnings call that it will start selling Cybercabs to fleet operators by the end of this year.
Broader expansion of the Cybercab could set up a real fight with Waymo, which is currently the market leader for robotaxis in the United States, with more than 4,000 of them deployed across more than a dozen cities. Tesla has argued that its Cybercab is cheaper and easier to build, which should allow it to undercut Waymo and other robotaxi operators on price. But the company has to reach real scale outside Austin in order to prove that point.
Tesla said it’s ready thanks to a dramatic increase in the number of miles its self-driving cars have traveled in recent weeks. While that may be true, Tesla was mum on Wednesday about how much money the overall robotaxi effort is bringing in. Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the new ride-hailing business won’t be noticeable in the company’s overall financial figures until the second quarter of 2027, “and probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year.”
Tesla also made a change to its letter to shareholders that further obscures what little visibility there was into its robotaxi business.
In Tesla’s second-quarter letter, the company included a chart for “Cumulative Paid Robotaxi Miles.” A close read of that chart showed a 36% decline from the first quarter of the year. In the new letter released on Wednesday, Tesla changed that chart to show “Cumulative Unsupervised Robotaxi Miles” — an indicator of how far the fleet cars are driving, whether or not they have paying riders on board.
There wasn’t much more clarity on the call, either. When asked about paid robotaxi miles traveled, Taneja said the company is “seeing utilization improving,” but didn’t offer specifics.
Instead, Taneja kept most of his comments generally focused on Tesla’s plans to scale the Cybercab. That included praise for Tesla’s engineering team for creating a vehicle that, according to the manufacturing team, is very easy to build — and build quickly.
“They think this is one of the easiest products for them to scale in terms of manufacturing,” he said. “So scaling would not be that much of a challenge.”
What might be a challenge, Taneja said, is that Tesla needs to make sure it has “all the regulatory approvals” so it can “start deploying the Cybercabs as fast as we can produce them.” That echoes many previous comments from Musk, who has long claimed that “regulatory approval” was the biggest barrier to Tesla’s robotaxi plans, not technical progress.
Musk has always been a bit hazy about what approvals, specifically, he felt were needed. The company has run into a regulatory hurdle this year, though. In September, just hours after Tesla formally launched its Cybercab in Austin, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an investigation into whether the vehicle complies with current federal motor vehicle safety standards.
All automakers self-certify that their vehicles conform to these standards, and Tesla has claimed that the Cybercab is compliant. But it is missing features that the current standards require, like a brake pedal and side mirrors. The NHTSA has proposed removing some of these requirements, but that rule change is likely still at least a few months away.
Not every Tesla executive agreed on this during Wednesday’s call.
Asked about the remaining bottlenecks for a wider robotaxi rollout, Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s vice president overseeing autonomy, said they are “not purely regulatory.”
“It’s technology-driven,” he said. “We had initially had the robotaxi service from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., and then expanded to 10 p.m. to 11 p.m, now it’s going to be pretty soon, [to] 2 a.m. So we’re slowly expanding the availability of robotaxi, and that is driven by the capability of the AI software.”
That could be why Tesla’s service still doesn’t operate on highways, and in certain conditions, although it has been spotted operating in heavy rain many times in Austin — something Waymo’s robotaxis have largely avoided. Elluswamy said Wednesday that Tesla plans to tackle more of these challenging driving scenarios by the end of this year, before scaling further.
“We just want to make sure that there’s not a single safety incident. That is our operating principle. And even if there’s the slightest possible risk at all, we don’t like to take on that risk,” he said.

title_en: iPhone Duo's next-gen prototypes are trying to cram in Face ID
title_fa: iPhone Duo's next-gen prototypes are trying to cram in Face ID
excerpt_en: Apple's first foldable phone opted for a feature it replaced on most iPhone models nearly 10 years ago.
excerpt_fa: Apple's first foldable phone opted for a feature it replaced on most iPhone models nearly 10 years ago.
content_en:
iPhone Duo's next-gen prototypes are trying to cram in Face ID
For understandable reasons, the first generation returned to Touch ID.
You might have a hard time trying to get hold of one yourself for the foreseeable future, but the iPhone Duo has been in the hands of reviewers for a little while now. And while it is clearly a first-generation product, overall impressions of Apple's first foldable have been broadly very positive.
One potential annoyance for anyone coming from another modern iPhone, however, is the lack of Face ID, with Apple instead opting to go back to Touch ID for the first time since 2022's iPhone SE. Most iPhone users will have been using Face ID since the iPhone X. In our own review we said the Touch ID solution here works accurately, but can take a bit longer to unlock the phone than you might expect, and according to reliable Apple insider Mark Gurman, the company is already looking at how it can bring its newer technology to the iPhone Duo's inevitable follow-up.
Speaking on his new Power On podcast, Gurman said Apple is "actively working" on under-display Face ID, and that there are already iPhone Duo 2 prototypes that have the technology built into the phone's outer display. He also pointed to the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, with their shrunken down Dynamic Island hardware, as evidence that Apple is finding ways to move more components underneath its phones' displays. The first-gen iPhone Duo also features Apple's first under-display camera.
As for why Apple chose to outfit its $2,000 foldable with a feature it largely retired from iPhones almost a decade ago (although plenty of MacBook and lower-end iPad models still use Touch ID), it likely has a lot to do with the fact the iPhone Duo is designed to be used in a number of different orientations. Putting Face ID sensors on both the inner and outer displays might have been a bit of a stretch, and may have pushed up the price of an already enormously expensive device.
Gurman points out that the iPhone Duo's display is very thin, so squeezing even more components into it would have also been challenging. Apple wanted uniformity with both displays, so getting Face ID into one but not the other was unlikely to materialize this time. The Bloomberg reporter added that the action button, which Apple introduced on the iPhone 15 Pro, may also feature in an eventual iPhone Duo 2.

title_en: Insta360 Mic review: A midrange mic kit that's anything but boring
title_fa: Insta360 Mic review: A midrange mic kit that's anything but boring
excerpt_en: In an ocean of boring microphones, Insta360's Mic adds a (customizable) pop of color.
excerpt_fa: In an ocean of boring microphones, Insta360's Mic adds a (customizable) pop of color.
content_en:
Insta360 Mic review: A midrange mic kit that's anything but boring
In an ocean of boring microphones, Insta360 adds a (customizable) pop of color.
It's been a transformative year for Insta360. The Luna Ultra and Luna Pro cameras, both released over the summer, cemented its reputation as a capable camera-maker that isn't limited to 360 video. When it unveiled the Mic Pro, with its quirky e-ink display, the portfolio of creator products was almost complete. Well, almost, because there was a small gap between the $330 Mic Pro and the affordable Mic Air.
Insta360 plugs that gap today with the $250 Mic. Yep, capital M as that's the full name of the product (let's just accept right now this review might get confusing). The Mic is a pared-down version of the Mic Pro, with a cost-saving feature that might actually make it more appealing to many creators. Wireless mic systems are plentiful, but the Insta360 Mic is curious and endearing. The question is, will that be enough to earn it a place on your lapel?
Insta360 Mic design and features
I loved the sound on Insta360's Mic Pro and it appears the regular Mic inherited the same audio quality. My voice isn't deep, but it's lower in register and I'm prone to swallowing my words. Recordings with the Mic on default settings and voice mode all sound as clear as a mumbling Brit like me could hope for. Activating the Rich voice tone adds a pleasing amount of presence when speaking, and is, dare I say it, more podcast-friendly. The Bright preset is better for outdoor recording when there's more ambient noise and you want your voice to stand out more, or if you have a particularly low voice, but the standard recording mode remains my preference.
Insta360's noise reduction also fares well in both indoor and outdoor environments, without any noticeable artifacting or impact on your voice as can sometimes be the case, especially with cheaper microphones. I prefer to leave any processing to the tools I have on my PC, but the noise cancellation is useful if you're recording in a noisy location and want to share a recording from your phone straight away.
I have a few Insta360 cameras — an Ace Pro 2, a Luna Ultra and a Luna Pro — and connecting the Mic directly is easy through on-camera menus. The receiver dongle on the Mic and Mic Pro is pretty chonky and looks conspicuous on a small camera or phone, so being able to ditch it completely is something I really appreciate.
One of the more interesting features is the ability to connect four microphones to one receiver. This is great for group interviews or even simple podcasts, especially as you can output each mic to its own audio channel for detailed editing in post. There's also a multi-receiver option, and it's a bit of a hidden gem. I often shoot with two cameras and having my voice record to both at the same time via two receivers saves me some time in editing as I no longer need to worry about keeping a master audio track and syncing the second camera — the audio I want is baked-in to both angles. You can also get creative with this and use a second mic to record ambient sound or another sound source for extra flexibility.
Insta360 Mic SD card support
On the one hand, the lack of onboard storage is a concession for the lower price. But by introducing removable memory, Insta360 has arguably given the Mic an advantage over the Pro. For starters, you're not limited to the amount of storage built-in to the device, so you can add a large SD card and get many more hours of on-board recording. It also means you can swap out a card should it ever fill up without having to transfer or delete files to make space. Working with additional SD cards is often simpler than connecting the mic via USB to access files. If there are any negatives, it does open up the chance of forgetting your SD card when you need it, and there's the small chance of dust ingress or mechanical failure. But honestly, I feel this is more of a Pro-grade feature in disguise.
That screen
The e-ink display on the Pro was Insta360's main selling point, and it's just as fun here on the regular Mic. I've heard some people complain about the size of the Mic/Mic Pro transmitters, and they sure are larger than rivals like DJI's Mic 3 or GoPro. However, they are the perfect size for displaying your show's logo, or whatever else you want to upload. It also opens up some creative and even interactive options to drive engagement with your audience if you make videos for YouTube and social media.
The competition
Take your pick: Rode, DJI, Hollyland and even GoPro. There are multiple options available for creators at various price points. Insta360 is selling the full kit (two transmitters, receiver and case) for $250 which puts it right between Rode's two most popular models: the Wireless Go III and the Wireless Pro. The former is popular, but it's awkward for connecting to phones, while the latter comes with two wired lav mics for a more complete "kit."
DJI's most recent mic kits are harder to find in the US, but the popular Mic 3 offers similar functionality to Insta360 with smaller, more discrete transmitters for about the same price. Neither Rode nor DJI have a customizable display, though. Hollyland's Lark 2 kit remains an incredibly popular choice and has similar-sized transmitters, and at $70 it's a staggering value. If you spring for the $300 Lark Max 2, you get wireless monitoring and a slew of other extras. Just remember: The Insta360's Mic and SD card slot remain the main differentiator here.
Wrap-up
Insta360 knew there was a lot of competition when it launched the Mic Pro. Functionally, it competes well with its rivals, and the e-ink display was a smart addition to make it stand out. With the regular Mic, the Pro's best features remain in a more economical package. The switch from on-board storage to SD card feels smart as it lowers cost while adding genuine practical advantages.
But that competition is real. If you just want two microphones and a...
